FOREWORD
WORDS OF DR. ROB STEPHEN, PRESIDENT OF CIGRE

                                  CIGRE is an organization that provides solu-
                                  tions to members on any aspects of the power
                                  delivery system from the output of the gener-
                                  ator to beyond the meter. It achieves this by
                                  forming working groups with international
                                  experts supplied by their companies to solve
                                  problems of mutual interest. The problems are
                                  identified and analyzed by Study Committees
                                  covering all aspects of power delivery. CIGRE
                                  has 16 such study committees with around 230
                                  working groups active at any one time. There
 Rob Stephen, President of CIGRE
                                  are over 3000 experts who are members of the
          (2016–2020)
                                  working groups busy solving the problems for
the benefit of the industry. CIGRE then produces technical brochures describ-
ing the solutions for all stakeholder to employ in their area.
Members of CIGRE come from over 90 countries. The Board of CIGRE, the
Administrative Council, consists of heads of National committees representing
different countries. There are 60 National committees (at time of writing). The
National committees ensure that information from the Study Committees is
disseminated to members in their country. They also arrange conferences and
invite working groups and Study Committees to meet in their countries to
expose the international experts to their local engineers.
In some cases, it was found beneficial to group a number of countries together
either due to language or geographical area to form a Region. Within a Re-
gion a sub structure of CIGRE is formed and topics pertinent to the Region
are discussed and resolved. Such a Region is the South East European Region
of CIGRE or SEERC. It was formed in 2013 and consists of 17 countries in the
Region which are geographically close.
This book covers the history of electricity within each country as well as the
history of CIGRE and the activities of CIGRE in their country. It is important to
have such a record to ensure future generations are aware of the progress made
and continue to make in the setting up of the Region and the events benefitting
members and the industry.



                                                                              xiii
The importance of CIGRE in the changing power generation and delivery en-
vironment cannot be underestimated. In the era of competition and evolving
technologies, technical information and solutions to problems are not readily
available or published. CIGRE forms a critical role in enabling information shar-
ing and problem solving across competitor and country lines. This benefits all
stakeholders including the end customer who can be assured that the methods
and technology implemented is of the highest standard. Engineers also have
a platform in which to network and share ideas which otherwise would have
been impossible to achieve.
With the 4th industrial revolution underway and new challenges being experi-
enced daily by utilities and energy providers; it is almost impossible to envisage
resolving problems faced today without CIGRE. I have often stated that at a
Study Committee meeting with international experts present, there is not a
problem that you may think of that has not already been solved or can be solved
with the expertise in the room.
I would like to thank the organizers and authors of this book that has made it
possible to reflect on the history of this important Region and provide a better
understanding of the countries that participate in the SEERC Region.
                                                                  28th February 2020


WORDS OF PROF. DR. KLAUS FRÖHLICH, PRESIDENT OF CIGRE
(2012 – 2016) AND ONE OF THE FOUNDING FATHERS OF SEERC

                                     When CIGRE was founded in Paris in Novem-
                                     ber 1921 it was intended to be a conference for
                                     sharing knowledge and discussion of problems
                                     concerning the electric power system. Not too
                                     many countries were contributing. Probably
                                     nobody at this time would envision an organi-
                                     sation which in the future would spread all over
                                     the globe becoming the number one platform
                                     for elaboration, dissemination and share of
                                     expertise in the field. Nowadays, almost one
                                     hundred years later history tells us an extraor-
      Klaus Fröhlich, President of   dinary success story. CIGRE quickly developed
               CIGRE                 into an organisation with the bi-annual con-
             (2012–2016)             ference in Paris and successive installation of


xiv
work bodies. Mission and basic set up of the organisation did not change during
the almost 100 years of existence. However, what has changed significantly is
the size in terms of contributing countries, membership numbers and the work
volume created by around 250 international working groups. Today CIGRE has
members in more than 90 countries and more than 60 National Committees
spread all over the globe. CIGRE by definition being an unpolitical institution
crosses all political barriers which fact enables the organisation to operate with
global significance. This way CIGRE’s contribution has been most instrumental
for the development of the electrical power system as we know it today.
Normally CIGRE deals with topics on an international worldwide basis. How-
ever, in places it seemed beneficial to cluster National Committees having a
common ground in terms of geographical situation, language and/or econom-
ical interest. Therefore, in accordance with the CIGRE Administrative Council
the so-called Regional CIGRE organisations were established – Asia-Australia
(AORC) in 2000, Northern Europe (NRCC) in 2001 and South America includ-
ing Spain and Portugal (RIAC) in 2006. Finally, in 2013 the South-East European
Region of CIGRE was added (SEERC). The foundation of the SEERC clearly
reflects the needs of this area for intensified cooperation. At the constituent
meeting of the SEERC in Montenegro in 2013 it was a pleasure for me to see how
CIGRE can provide a neutral platform for engineers and scientists smoothing
discrepancies in interest and political opinion of the various participants.
After foundation of the SEERC the participating National Committees started
with amazing efforts and speed. They have convincingly demonstrated by nu-
merous meetings and a number of successful conferences that regional prob-
lems are dealt with in a most fruitful way. These events have been providing not
only technical/scientific gain, but they also enhance visibility for the benefit of
CIGRE in the various countries. Being president of CIGRE at this time I offer
my respect and compliments to SEERC’s efficient performance. The “SEERC
book” as presented here is a perfect opportunity to learn more about the region.
Historical facts concerning the origins of electricity show that the region was
a sort of a cradle for the electric power system. Information about the work
of SEERC and their achievements provided as well. History and profile of the
power system in the various participating countries provide information of
common interest. The book is an expression of joint efforts of the SEERC Na-
tional Committees. In view of CIGRE’s one hundred anniversary next year it is
a most welcomed contribution of the SEERC. Congratulations on this excellent
work to the authors of this book.
                                                                    26th June 2020

WORDS OF PHILIPPE ADAM, SECRETARY GENERAL OF CIGRE

                                  At the time this book is published, 44 CIGRE
                                  National Committees (72%) are members of
                                  one of the four CIGRE regions. CIGRE SEERC
                                  is the largest, with 17 National Committees and
                                  18 countries.
                                  These numbers show the great interest that Na-
                                  tional Committees have for this organization
                                  between the global and national levels.
                                  CIGRE Regions are essential and instrumen-
                                  tal to develop events and activities around the
                                  planet on behalf of the global association.
 Philippe Adam, Secretary General
            (Since 2014)          This is because it is much easier for a Region
                                  than for a National Committee to reach the
critical mass to convene a large conference, in terms of scientific and technical
support and expected attendance.
Among the about 100 events organized by CIGRE every year, if we exclude the
Paris Session and two symposia which are supported logistically by the Central
Office, the largest are organized by the Regions, in addition to the many other
events organized by National Committees individually.
They allow to address subjects that may not be seen with the same interest from
a global perspective, but which are very important at regional level.
In addition to convening conferences, Regions are free to create specific Work-
ing Groups provided that they inform the Technical Council of their proposals
so that eventually a global response could be considered.
Regions are also the adequate solution to disseminate the findings and news
from the Paris Session that cannot be attended by all CIGRE members, if we
consider our statistics which show that less than 25% of CIGRE members reg-
ister to the Session.
Created in 2013 SEERC is the most recent Region of CIGRE, and has the dyna-
mism of its youth. Since its creation seven new members have joined its found-
ing members, and the third biennial conference was ready to be held in June
2020 when the pandemic due to the SARS CoV2 led the organizing committee
to postpone it to 2021.
The preparation of this book is another proof of that dynamism, and it is a
great honor for me to have been invited to write a few words to celebrate its
publication.

BAKIC who is so passionate and knowledgeable with the History in general,
and in particular the history of electricity.




OPENING REMARKS
                                   This book tells us the story of the history
                                   and activities in the life of electrical systems
                                   in the countries of Central, Southern and
                                   Eastern Europe, which represent one of the
                                   world’s regions of CIGRE. Representatives of
                                   these countries are their national committees
                                   CIGRE, which are part of the history of the de-
                                   velopment of these electrical power systems.
                                   All these national electrical power systems are
                                   interconnected to each other and create part of
         Kresimir Bakic
                                   the global interconnection that is the greatest
                                   engineering achievement of mankind in the
twentieth century. Global electrical interconnection is a great machine without
which modern life would almost be impossible, as Neil Armstrong, first man
on the Moon, stated in his speech in February 2000. In the creation of this
machine, CIGRE has played an important unifying role in the last century.
After 2000, Association CIGRE has expanded so wide around the world that it
has demonstrated the need to establish regions. Their purpose was to further
expand expert knowledge through additional activities. Region SEERC is rep-
resenting early history of electrification in each member country and present
activities of National Committees as well future plans.
The story really started in 1800 with the discovery of an electric battery and
thus current electricity (or galvanic electricity), by the outstanding genius of
physics, Professor Alessandro Volta, at Pavia University in Northern Italy. Eighty
years later the focus of electricity inventions was on multiphase AC systems as
system which enables wide electrification with economical advantages, where
we met two extraordinary inventors from SEERC region (Tesla, Ferraris) as well
AC pioneer company Ganz. For those reasons experts from SEERC region are



                                                                               xvii
responsible to participate as much as possible in creation of the future power
system.
Why is history of electricity so important? Having knowledge of our history
allows us to understand where we are coming from, which in turn allows us to
understand our present. It not only reveals the past, but it also helps us create
a better future. An understanding of the successes and failures of the past is
important to make progress going forward. And today electric systems faces
major challenges of future design to decarbonization of power system. For this
reason we discuss near future changes with penetration of Renewable sources
in the system. History of each system was prepared by experts coming exclu-
sively from each SEERC member state. It is the value of this book.
CIGRE is a truly great technical organization, growing like family with selfless
mutual support of each member and the desire to share knowledge and expe-
riences. This is what young engineers need more than pure theoretical confer-
ences. CIGRE is like post-academic education in electric power development
and operation. Those exact words were used my old CIGRE friend Jack Casazza
some thirty years ago, when we discussed the value of CIGRE.
The concept of the book was to present the life of the SEERC region by the third
conference in June 2020 and the development of electrification by country that
make up this region of CIGRE. Therefore, the historical boundary is defined
in June 2020.
                                                                Kresimir Bakic
                                                             Editor & co-author

1. INTRODUCTION – The first 100 years of CIGRE

1.1 Beginning of electricity and knowledge dissemination before
CIGRE

Mankind needed almost 200 years (17th and 18th century) from first hypotheses
about new natural phenomenon, with name “electricity”, coined from Greek
name of amber (W. Gilbert, T. Browne), to a recognition of static electricity and
invention of second form of electricity also called current (or galvanic) electricity
(by A. Volta, in year 1800), which significantly accelerated and changed the world.

The first awareness of the importance of electricity for wider use in society
began in the year 1831, after the ingenious discovery of the phenomenon of
electro-magnetic induction by Michael Faraday. It was possible to produce
current electricity using mechanically powered generators converting me-
chanical energy. Next year, Hyppolite Pixii used steel magnets to build the
first generator exploiting the induction effect. As generators improved over the
years, they were used to operate arc lights and other uses. The dynamo-electric
principle, discovered almost simultaneously and independently by Werner
Siemens, Charles Wheatstone, and Alfred Varley, giving a strong boost to the
development of use of electricity. In 1860, Antonio Pacinotti, invented an im-
proved form of direct-current electrical generator, which he described in a
paper published in Il Nuovo Cimento of 1865. It used a ring armature around
which was wrapped a coil of wire, to produce a smoother current, than that
available from previous types of dynamo. He found that the device could also
be used as an electric motor. Next year in 1866, Werner Siemens, after his com-
pany invented dynamo generator (DC) and believed that “self-excitement” or
dynamo-electric principle would play a major role in generating electric energy
in the future. He supposedly coined the word “electro-technique”, meaning the
complete application of electricity with generating, distributing, and using
electrical devices. In that early years of applicable electricity, all progress, and
dissemination of technical news were presented at different exhibitions all
over the Europe and world.

The only well-known institution with reputation of transactions was the Royal
Society (UK) and after 1800 the Royal Institution, where M. Faraday was em-
ployed. This institution played a particularly important role in dissemination


                                                                                              1
SEERC CIGRE HISTORY




of electricity knowledge in the 19th century. National Technical Societies dealing
exclusively with electricity progress, began with active work in second part
of the 19th century, i.e. well-known as the IEE (British Institute for Electrical
Engineers), that was founded in 1871, as the Society of Telegraph Engineers,
which changed its name in 1880 to the Society of Telegraph Engineers and
Electricians and in 1889 changed name again to the Institution of Electrical
Engineers (IEE) or similar society American Institute of Electrical Engineers
(AIEE), which was established in 1884 and later merged with the Institute of
Radio Engineers and in 1963 renamed to today well-known IEEE, etc. In those
years have been established national societies for Electrical Engineering in
many countries worldwide.

At the end of the nineteenth century, the knowledge of Electrotechnical novel-
ties was transferred mainly at the World Fairs or special International Expo-
sitions of electricity. The first, so called International Exposition of Electricity
took place in Paris, in 1881. This event was associated with International Con-
gress organized by French Government, led by Minister of Posts and Telecom-
munications, Mr. Adolphe Cochery and ordered by the president Jules Grévy. In
opening speech, he expressed the great interest to clarify the state of electrical
science and its applications, and to draw together and compare the results of
research. It was first ever comprehensive international gathering of electrical
technologies to take place (called “Congres International des Électriciens”), dis-
cussing on topics of springing up electricity science /R.8/. Congress was highly
attended, with more than 250 experts and the most advanced world’s scien-
tists from 27 countries, e.g. Werner Siemens, H. Helmholtz, G. R. Kirchhoff,
Z. Gramme, Jablochoff, H. Fontaine, M. Deprez, Lord Kelvin, G. Ferraris, etc.
World population at that time was 1.5 billion.

Marcel Deprez presented new principles of electrical circuit operation – par-
allel scheme, which was contrary to previous series operation due to needs of
constant current for arc lights. New principle opened the door to commercial
use of electricity with different customers. At congress scientists for the first
time discussed many interesting subjects and had international discussions
on electricity units. They recommended the ampere, volt and ohm as practical
units for current, voltage and resistance, which were generally adopted by elec-
trical engineers. It was clear that the International Exhibition and Congress in
Paris in 1881 showed very advanced stage of study of the development of the
DC machines.


2
              Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




It is very interesting, and not by chance that exactly 40 years later in Paris was
CIGRE established, which continued international congress for supporting
electricity technology development, standardization of new equipment for
electrical systems and exchange of technical information on electric power
systems in a spirit of cooperation, impartiality and service.

Next year in 1882, on September 4th, in New York, Pearl Street Power Station
began working, the first commercial electric power plant, operating with six
dynamos (600 kW) fired by coal, and serving 82 customers with about 400
light bulbs (DC – direct current). Thus, electricity became a business.
In the same year, on September 16th, in Munich, Second International Exposi-
tion of Electricity was organized, where they demonstrated the transmission of
electric power with direct current (DC) on long-distance of 57 km, from Mies-
bach to Munich. The project was designed by French electrician Marcel Deprez
and German pioneer of electricity Oscar von Müller, who in 1903 established,
the largest technical museum in the world, located in Munich (“Deutsches
Museum von Meisterwerken der Naturwissenschaft und Technik”). The pro-
ject used voltage level of 2 kV, with power transmitted 2.5 kW, with which an
artificial waterfall ran. They used a simple iron telegraph wire, which failed a
few days later. Efficiency of the transmission was extremely low and confirmed
that DC transmission on longer distances is not economical.
However, in the same year 1882, a new idea was born to approach an operation
of current electrical systems, using polyphase AC systems. Many historians
of electrical technologies used to say, that the period from 1882 to 1892 was
the most innovatory period in history, which enabled later the development
of massive electricity use. First attempt of this approach belongs to famous
inventor Nikola Tesla. After the rumors runs by generations of people coming
from Nikola Tesla homeland (Smiljan, region of Lika, Croatia), there is also ex-
planation of where and how Nikola Tesla got this wonderful idea of multiphase
AC system. During Tesla’s work in Budapest, in 1882, Tesla took a rest one
afternoon in the Budim Fisherman’s Bastion, watching Donau River bathing
in the sun. The waves on water were flowing synchronously with sunshine
glitters atop of each wave. Twenty-six years old Tesla suddenly got an idea about
similarities of transmitting power of Donau water with power in electrical
machines by electro-magnetic waves. After that, he was obsessed with the
idea of multi-wave systems and the thought of making it. Later, he developed
model in his mind. This story was passing by generations from people close
to him. The fact is that many scientists drew their ideas from nature. During


                                                                                              3
SEERC CIGRE HISTORY




Tesla’s work for Edison in Paris, just before he moved to USA in 1884, he made
a presentation in Strasbourg on the model of 2-phase synchronous generator
and motor connected with 4 conductors. However, invention of polyphase
systems was not simple and passed vivid history, which somebody called “first
technological war” or “war of currents” between DC and polyphase AC.




            Fig. 1.1 Nikola Tesla              Fig. 1.2 Prof. Galileo Ferraris

In 1883, in Vienna, was the Third International Exposition of Electricity. On
September 17th work started parallel to the exhibition of the scientific Commis-
sion having its purpose in taking of electrical measurements and conducting
scientific research at the Exhibition. The elected president of the Commission
was Professor Josef Stefan (Vienna) and as vice-presidents Professor Galileo
Ferraris (Turin), Professor Hauffe (Vienna), Professor Kittler (Darmstadt), Sir
William Siemens (London), etc. Commission was subdivided in eight sections
according to the matters it concerned, i.e. scientific instruments, dynamo elec-
tric machines, electric lighting, transmission of power, telegraphy, telephony,
etc. The public attendance on Universal Exhibition was exceptionally large, in
average 15,000 visitors daily. The interest and impact of this event in Vienna
to the whole region was enormous. Many countries in region started with first
electric projects just after Vienna International Exposition.
Next important event in history of electricity was the Exposition of Electricity
in 1884, in Turin (Italy). Based on the ideas of Galileo Ferraris, they made a
single-phase AC transmission of 20 kW, 2000 V on 40 km distance, but with-
out a motor. The efficiency of this long-distance transmission was 89%. The


4
                  Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




results of this attempt shown that AC transmission of electric power is relatively
simple and with high efficiency. The open question was the AC motor, which
could have at least similar performances as the DC motor. This great challenge
has been tackled by many researchers like Tesla, Bradley, Haselwander, Ferraris,
Dolivo-Dobrovolsky, Wenstrom, etc. Due to historically very important inventions
for later electrification of world following section try to describe little be more
details about this amazing decade 1882 –1892.

on polyphase systems happened all over the world.

Sometimes someone try to reveal historic truth, asking themselves who is the
real inventor of inventions. In /R.11/, remarkably interesting statement on that
subject was: “There is a different long journey between discovery and realization
of invention. If an invention was created in the time when the elements for real-
ization are not yet known, the authors of the realization and invention are both
- inventor and creator of product. However, if the invention was created in the
time when the elements of realization are known, the author of the invention is
only an inventor”. After 1884 many worldwide scientists were dealing with poly-
phase systems and motors. Many of them deserve to be remembered because
the world would be different without these researchers and great geniuses.

Good analysis and chronology of invention of polyphase system and basic ele-
ments was investigated by German VDE (Verband Deutscher Elektrotechniker)
in 1957–1959 /R.12, Hillebrand/.

The first published attempts with rotating magnetic fields were presented in
1883 by Marcel Deprez, but unfortunately this famous electrician stopped too


6
               Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




early with research on that topic. First attempts of the model for 2-phase in-
ductive motor construction was made by G. Ferraris in 1885 /R 12,16/, but he
unfortunately believed incorrectly that such motors can never exceed an effi-
ciency of 50%, so he lost interest in continuing to develop this kind of machine.
Anyhow, he offered his work freely to the service of mankind and for many other
researchers it was a great challenge (i.e. Dolivo-Dobrovolski, as he stated in an
interview). Table 1.1a and 1.1b present chronology of the inventions and patents
of polyphase systems by different authors in period 1882–1892.

In conclusion of report /R.12/ author approved that Tesla was first who inten-
sively dealt with electric power transmission using polyphase alternating cur-
rent (AC) system and he was the first who described fundamentals of such
transmission and the first who patented principle of polyphase induction mo-
tor. Report also states that in this period 1882–1892 the solution of the problem
was almost in the air, so it is not surprising that similar paths of thought were
formed in many minds, almost simultaneously with similar solutions. However,
both initiators of invention, Tesla and Ferraris, were very generous and freely
opened great ideas to all mankind, which caused dissemination of technical
novelty and acceleration of development polyphase systems as well as compe-
tition. Nikola Tesla was not only a great scientist, but also a great humanist,
namely a Human. Professor Milan Vidmar (“father” of the Slovenian electric
power system) after met him in New York in 1936 was very happy to meet titan
of the electrical profession, and described him with following words “as an artist,
a poet, who suffer when he creates, who is moving away from the world, who despises
money, does not care for foolish titles and awards, who lives for his ideas and does not
need comfort or luxury; he is exactly that”.
Unfortunately, Professor Galileo Ferraris died too early (February 7, 1897), only
50 years old, in time of his most powerful research capability. He left the first
theoretical explanation of the operation of rotating magnetic fields to mankind
(Un metodo per la trattazione del vettori rotanti od alternativi ed una applicazione di
esso motori elettrici a correnti alternate, Torino, March 1888). For that reason, many
historians defined him as a main researcher for rotating AC fields since he
first constructed a two-phase motor and explained the invention in March 1888
during academic lecture in Turin.
In history of electricity there are well-known inventions, which were patented,
but not publicized enough in professional community and for this reason re-
mained unknown. For example, a Canadian invention “Method and apparatus
for controlling electric current” from 1925 patented by Julius Edgar Lilienfeld, a


                                                                                               7
SEERC CIGRE HISTORY




physicist born in the Austro-Hungarian Empire in Lemberg (known today as
Lvov, Ukraine), who invented the actual version of primitive transistor (Lilien-
feld proposed three-electrode structure, using copper-sulphide semiconduc-
tor material). More than 15 years later transistor was invented name coined
and patented by three American inventors (Bardeen, Shockley, and Brattain).
They received a Nobel Prize for that in 1956. From this example we can see the
important role Ferraris and Tesla played, giving openly their own ideas and
disseminated these ideas of polyphase electrical system to the world. This has
hastened important discoveries.
On the other hand, it is true, that German engineer Dolivo-Dobrovolsky, was
the first one, who constructed and applied the three-phase system, connected
in a star or delta, which requires just three power lines instead of four, and thus
is less expensive than a two-phase system. In August 1891, during International
Exposition of Electricity in Frankfurt AC three-phase system was demonstrated
for the first time in history as a long-distance transmission (175 km) between
Lauffen and exhibition place in Frankfurt. This project was designed by Mikhail
Dolivo-Dobrovolsky (1862–1919), Oskar von Miller (1855–1934) and Charles Lance-
lot Brown (1863–1924). Last one was from Machine Fabrik Oerlikon (MFO), Swit-
zerland. After this project in 1891, Brown with his friend Walter Boveri, founded
the company Brown-Boveri & Cie (BBC) in Baden, Switzerland, which became
a global industry and took Swiss industry an enormous step forward. In 1978,
BBC was merged with Swedish company ASEA to presently well-known company
ABB. The project presented in Frankfurt involved synchronous 3-phase genera-
tor located in Lauffen (output power 230 kVA, speed 150 rpm, 42 Hz and voltage
95 V, with windings in a star connection), which was designed and constructed
by C. Brown from MFO, with a step up transformer to 15 kV (prismatic magnetic
core filled with oil). Overhead line contained with wooden telegraph poles with
a span of 60 m, pin-type porcelain insulators filled with oil, copper conductors
with diameter 4 mm. In the location at exhibition in Frankfurt, was a step-down
transformer from 15 kV to 65 V and asynchronous 3-phase machine 100 HP,
which operated a small waterfall. The overhead line and motor were designed
and constructed by Dolivo-Dobrovolsky. International commission selected to
evaluate project reported on transmission of power with following results:
   • Efficiency of transmission was between 68.5% and 75.2%.
   • Voltage of OHL was tested from 15 kV to 25 kV and maximum efficiency
      was 78.9%.
Thus, the first 3-phase transmission of electric power approved victory of poly-
phase AC against overcame a DC transmission. This demonstration of 3-phase


8
              Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




transmission project in 1891 announced the beginning of electrification of
world.

Next polyphase project was made in 1895, and was proclaimed in the interna-
tional press more than any other electricity project. It was a construction of
Niagara Falls AC Power Plants with power transmission to Buffalo in USA, on
the distance of 30 km. Westinghouse Company won the contract to build power
plant and General Electric Company won the contract for power transmission
to Buffalo. Power plant (called Adams plant) at Niagara Falls was designed as
a 2-phase system with frequency 25 Hz. In substation it was converted to a
3-phase transmission system of 11 kV directed to Buffalo. Transmission pro-
ject started with operation one year later (1896). It is interesting that select-
ing commission leading by Lord Kelvin discussed of five different options for
transmission of power from Niagara Falls to Buffalo. One of the options was
transmission power using compressed air. Many historic files approved that
success of the 3-phase transmission project in Germany in 1891, was one of the
main reasons for decision of AC polyphase system for Adams power plant and
transmission power to Buffalo. Great popularity of this project was probably
due to an exceptionally large power plant of 37 MW (50000 HP) at that time.

Thus, at the beginning of 20th century it was clear that future of electrification
will run on a three-phase system. Electric energy definitely obtained an impor-
tant part in the further development of humankind. In the technological duel
between the direct current and alternating current, the form of alternating
polyphase current was winning, since it proved to be the most appropriate
form for broad use and economically more efficient. All inventors and creators
of a three-phase power system deserve a credit for world’s electrification and
enormous fast development of our civilization.

Beside exhibitions, electricity was disseminated also through books. In that
time particularly the “Julius Springer Publishing House” was specialized in
literature from the natural sciences and engineering. Springer’s publishing
activities promoted the rise of these disciplines, paving the way for the modern
knowledge-based society. In 1880s, they took over several scientific journals
that quickly became staples in the professional world, e.g. VDI (in 1882). In a
known inventive decade from 1882–1892, they published many books explaining
fundamentals of DC and AC electricity world.



                                                                                              9
SEERC CIGRE HISTORY




Elements such as generators, transformers, conductors, insulators, and sys-
temic questions on the performance of electrical current became the focus of
attention of the newly formed profession.
In addition, faculties for electrical engineering began to emerge. First university
in the world to set up a chair in electrical engineering was in Darmstadt (Ger-
many) in 1882, and in the next year, they founded the first faculty of electrical
engineering and introduced the world’s first-degree course in electrical engi-
neering. Thus, at the turn of the 19th to 20th century rose interest for commer-
cialization of the newest energy type – electric energy. For this reason, needs
for standardization become crucial.

In 1904, in St. Louis (USA), was an important International Electrical Exhibi-
tion with a first meeting of scientists with goal to establish an International
Electrotechnical Commission (IEC). In 2006, two years later, IEC was founded
to meet growing need to standardize the electricity machinery and emerging
home devices across the world. First president of IEC was Lord Kelvin (William
Thomson). Soon, in 1907–1908, domestic devices as electric vacuum cleaner,
washing machine were invented. Same year, vertical suspension string insula-
tor was invented in electricity transmission sector, which enabled construction
of OHLs over 60 kV, as well as first ACSR conductors (1907).
Next very important innovation was Ludwig Roebel’s generator bars, in 1912,
reducing loses in copper stator windings of AC generators. Roebel’s bars enabled
construction of much larger generators. All these innovations decreased cost
of electricity production and increased number of customers.

IEC started working in 1910 with technical committee (TC) 1 – Terminology, and
before first CIGRE conference in 1921, with another 7 technical committees (TC
2 – Rotating machinery, TC 3 – Information structures, and graphical symbols, TC
4&5 – Hydraulic and Steam turbines, TC 6 – Lamp sockets and caps, TC 7 Overhead
electrical bare conductors, and TC 8 – System aspects for electrical energy supply).
However, at beginning it was obvious, that further development and operation
of growing electric systems and market of elements and services requires more
international discussion on specific technical issues, harmonization of certain
approaches, solutions for frequency issues, sharing experiences, research works,
etc. All these issues led to emerging of new international electro-technical con-
ference.

               Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




  Who invented the transmission of electrical power?
  Frenchman Hippolyte Fontaine (1833–1910) was famous pioneer of electricity. He used
  to work with Gramme Society (Zenobe Gramme was famous Belgian electricity inventor).
  Dynamo invented by Z. Gramme in 1871, has been improved Siemens’s dynamo from 1866
  and the first in the world to provide a higher voltage and more stable direct current. At
  the World’s Fair of 1873 in Vienna, H. Fontaine wanted to show visitors how a water pump
  could operate powered by an electromagnetic machine using DC electricity produced by
  new invented Dynamo. In the beginning water pump did not work properly. He found out
  that resistivity of link had to be increase. From neighboring exhibitors than he borrowed
  missing copper wire (it was approx. 1000 m), connected dynamo with DC motor nearby to
  the water pump. And finally, the pump was working properly. “After this experiment”, said
  H. Fontaine, “I got an idea how mechanical power could be transmitted to distance by elec-
  tricity”. He wrote an article about it in a French newspaper. Fontaine’s idea was first used
  by the French sugar factory-owners Felix and Chretien in 1878, at its factory in Sermaises.
  Since the processing of sugar beet is seasonal work and except for one month in the rest of
  the year their steam machines usually stay unproductive. So, they decided to use its steam
  engines for useful work, for transfer of electrical power from factory halls to plowing fields.
  At a steam machine they installed dynamo to produce DC electricity and used flexible cable
  at a distance of 800 m (from the factory to the ground fields) to transmit power to the DC
  motor, which was specially developed for the plow plowing. This was the transmission of
  electrical power into the electric plowing in France, in 1878. That example found many im-
  itators in France and elsewhere, in particular because of the economic efficiency. Fontaine
  also played important role at the First World Electrotechnical Congress and Exhibition in
  Paris in 1881, and this story was discussed at the second session for public on October 4,
  1881 (see Reference 8, page 371).
  As a pioneer of electrical science, France awarded Hippolyte Fontaine the Legion of Honor,
  a high recognition.



Summary of milestones of growing electric power system before CIGRE was
established:

• 1800, Alessandro Volta was credited as the inventor of the electric
  battery, first source of current (galvanic) electricity. Today, we can say
  that this invention completely changed mankind.
• 1831, Michael Faraday, invented the principles of electromagnetic
  induction, enabling many applications in electricity such as
  transformers, electric motors, and generators.
• 1865, James Clerk Maxwell publication “A Dynamical Theory
  of the Electromagnetic Field", which summarized knowledge of
  electromagnetism with 20 fundamental equations. Around 1882,
  Oliver Heaviside uses vector calculus and reduces it to 4 equations
  with 4 variables. Those equations fully describe the theory of electrical
  engineering.

 • 1866, Werner Siemens develops the dynamo-electric machine based
   on the double-T armature. This invention makes the current electricity

   Alteneck (1873) improved a dynamo machine to produce a smooth DC

1.2 Short history of CIGRE

The IEC was responsible for the standardisation of equipment as an Interna-
tional Electrotechnical Committee for Standards, as well as the nomenclature
of electrical quantities and units and the definitions of terms. Its work required
the research support of international experts. Conferences were possible solu-
tion. With the help of another organisation, Union des Syndicats de l’Électricité
(USE) from Paris, which had offered its staff and facilities, the idea of estab-
lishing an international conference was close to its realisation. The USE rep-
resented French experts from electrical profession. Thus, in the year 1921, the
international organisation of CIGRE was founded as the result of the needs for
an international cooperation of experts, who would solve common problems in
creation of growing interconnected electrical system.


   First acronym CIGRÉ stood from French “Conférence Internationale des Grands Réseaux
   Électriques”, while after the year 2000 changed to “Conseil International des Grands Ré-
   seaux Électriques” and after 2016, CIGRE means just a brand of global organization dealing
   with a whole electricity sector.



Europe was quite demolished after the First World War and needed fast reno-
vation. Additionally, in the year 1920, severe drought had affected Europe. Great
investments had to be made into the new infrastructure were linked with the
beginnings of electrification. New views on connecting the small isolated elec-
trical systems of that time and mutual support of hydro and thermo-systems,
between Switzerland, France and Italy had emerged. Discussions on intercon-
nected electrical networks began. This called for new equipment standards. At
the same time, an international market for equipment was opening. This was an
opportunity to convene an International Conference. On 21st March 1921 in Par-
is, the Secretary General of the French Association of the Electrical Profession
(USE), Jean Tribot Laspiere, concluded an agreement with the President of the
IEC, Dr. Cyprien O’Dillon Mailloux, and the Secretary General of the IEC, Mr.
Charles Delacour Le Maistre in order to convene an International Conference
for large electrical networks.




                                                                                                13
SEERC CIGRE HISTORY




     Dr. Cyprien O’Dillon Mailloux (1860–1932) was the IEC president in between 1919–1923,
     and the director of the secretariat on nomenclature. He was president of AIEE in the period
     1913–1914. He had served as president for the American National Committee of the IEC
     during 1914–1924, as chairman of the advisors on nomenclature, as representative of
     the National Research Council on the division of foreign relations and honorary president.
     Charles Delacour Le Maistre (1874–1953) was first Secretary General of IEC, from 1906 until
     1953. He was awarded as Knight Commander of the Order of Vasa from UK and Chevalier of
     the Legion of Honour from France. His contribution to the IEC was as critical to the creation
     of the modern world as the work of the famous scientists or innovators and entrepreneurs.
     For more than forty years, he attended every meeting, managed its activities, and travelled
     the world as the ambassador of international standardization.
     Jean Tribot-Laspière (21 June 1882–10 May 1963) was Secretary General of USE (Union
     des Syndicats de l’Electricité) and from 1921 until his death Vice-president and Delegate
     General of CIGRE.


Upon recommendation by the IEC, the Conference was to address the issue of
transmission with high voltage and have a scientifically, technical, and usable
character. At that time, the highest voltage in the world was 120 kV, with some
experiments on 220 kV. After a six-month period of preparations, the first Con-
ference was convened and held in Paris from 21st to 26th November 1921, at the
USE headquarters. As this was an important Conference for the IEC, several
countries that were members of IEC participated. To the first conference 231
delegates from 12 countries had attended. The defeated countries of the First
World War were not invited and not allowed to participate in the Conference,
although Germany was highly developed in terms of electrical engineering
that time. For this reason, some historians considered CIGRE to be the “baby”
of the Entente, the winning alliance of the First World War. A Frenchman,
René Legouez, was elected as the first President of CIGRE (he remained in
this position up to the year 1928), who up to that time, was the President of the
USE, while Mr. Mailloux, the President of the IEC, was elected as the Honorary
President. Altogether, there were 64 reports submitted to the first Conference
and were discussed in three sections. At the First Conference there was no
discussion on permanence of this organisation.




          Fig. 1.3 Delegates at the first CIGRE Conference in Paris, November 21, 1921


14
              Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




The establishment of CIGRE must be considered in the context of searching
for new economic and technological directions on a wider international basis.
The difference between CIGRE and the IEC was, and still is, in the fact that
CIGRE presents individual opinions on a certain technical issue and not (as is
the case with IEC) nationally agreed standpoints. This gives the participants
at CIGRE the necessary freedom of thinking in professional debates and the
results of discussions on certain issues an added value. Advantage of CIGRE is
also cooperation of all sides dealing with electricity sector as Electricity Supply
Industry experts, Academia and Researching side and experts from Manufac-
turing Industry as well.

The 2nd CIGRE Session was held in 1923 (26th November to 1st December) at the
same place as the first conference. Three important decisions were accepted:
  • That Conferences should be convened biannually,
  • That National Committees for the collection of Reports would be estab-
      lished in each country (the first National Committees were British, Dutch,
      and Italian), and
  • That a Study Committee for the study of the “Rational Use of Energy would
      be established”.
From the Study Committee for the Rational Use of Energy emerged an idea
for the establishment of a wider international organisation of energy. In fact,
as early as 1924, World Energy Conference emerged from this CIGRE Study
Committee, known today as the World Energy Council – WEC.
Initially, it was called the World Power Conference and was founded in London
in 1924. The convener was Mr. Daniel Nicol Dunlop, who was later announced
to be the Founder. In the year 1968, at the Conference in Moscow, its name
was changed into World Energy Conference, and later on in the year 1992, at the
time of the Congress in Madrid, into its present name: The World Energy Council
(WEC). In the thirties, this organisation had an important role in directing the
development of global energetics.
Second CIGRE Session 375 delegates from 19 countries had attended. From
SEERC region came delegates from Italy (48), Turkey (2), Czechoslovakia (6)
and Hungary (1).

The 3rd CIGRE Session was in 1925, held on a new location in Paris. New venue
was at the Foundation Rothchild building. Number of participating countries
increased to 27 with 530 delegates. Important decision was made to establish
second Study Committee (SC) named “Statistics Generation Transmission”. This


                                                                                            15
SEERC CIGRE HISTORY




SC was functioning for a short time and was transferred into that time created
UNIPEDE association, which merged to EURELECTRIC in December 1999.


     UNIPEDE - Union internationale des producteurs et distributeurs d’énergie électrique, was
     International Union of Producers and Distributors of Electrical Energy, founded in 1925
     in Paris. In 1999, this organization was merged with European Grouping of the Electricity
     Supply Industry (EURELECTRIC).



The 4th CIGRE Session was in 1927, which was particularly important in the his-
tory of CIGRE, because it established several Study Committees, which became
later the focus of activities.
SC1 – Isolating oils and insulating materials,
SC2 – HV Cables
SC3 – Interrupters (or later named Circuit breakers),
SC x – Improvement of the Power factor (Reactive power compensation), and
SC xx – Parallel Operation.
Last two SCs were without numbers.
From fourth Session 1927 until the ninth Session in 1939, CIGRE events were
held in the Salle Hoche (Avenue Hoche). In 1928 second president of CIGRE was
selected. It was Marcel Ulrich from France.

5th CIGRE Session in 1929 continued with the rising of the participants. In the
following table 1.1, increasing number of countries and delegates are shown in
the first 5 Sessions.

6th Session in 1931, was important due to the first registration of CIGRE as a
non-governmental organization in accordance with the French law. The first
Statutes of CIGRE was approved on 18th June 1931. It was published in an old
Electra issue no. 3 in November 1931.


16
                Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




First Statute of CIGRE defined international association as permanent with a
name “Conférence Internationale des Grands Réseaux Électriques” based on French
law from 1st July 1901. The head office was in Paris, at address Marceau 54.
Following paragraph defined a field of activities at biannual conferences under
the aegis of IEC. International cooperation between conferences was stated in
Statutes as follows:
  • Construction and operation of central power stations and substations,
  • Design, construction, insulation, and operation of the OHLs,
  • Operation, protection, and integration of power systems.
Important stipulation in the Statute was the following statement “organization
and support of friendly technical cooperation between associations, administrations,
engineers, scientists, and manufacturers of all countries”. Cooperation with other
international organizations was highlighted in the first Statute.
In Paragraph 11 the basis for creation of National Committees of CIGRE was
stated, administrative role of communication between individual and collec-
tive members and central control bodies of CIGRE. It is safe to say, that main
framework of CIGRE as independent organization was established in 1931.
CIGRE became autonomous, that the administrative organization of the con-
ferences was no longer supported by the USE as was the case since 1921. In 1931,
SC 6 for Overhead lines was also established.

In 1933 a Frenchman, E. Mercier, who was an exceptionally gifted engineer, a
builder of numerous power facilities, an innovator and a leading protagonist
within the World Energy Conference (WEC) and the World Trade Organisation
(WTO), became the President of the Paris CIGRE. He provided the organisa-
tion with a new momentum in this crucial period. His Presidential mandate
was the longest thus far, comprising of 15 years. He was also known for his
renowned statement that CIGRE was the spirit of the development of electric
power systems, which still is true today. His successors – Presidents of CIGRE,
were always very esteemed and reputable experts in the world’s energetics. This
is still the case today.


   Thus, CIGRE is not only a state of mind. It also represents a type of spirit, a spirit which has
   often been called the CIGRE spirit.
                                                  – E. Mercier, president of CIGRE (1933–1948)

The number of participants grew with time, from 231 to 870, while the number
of participating countries grew from 12 to 46. In the year 1937 at the 9th Session,
it was the highest number of delegates counting up to 870; from SEERC region
area came 9 countries and today 17, with 144 delegates or 17%.

The 10th Session was held just 3 months before the beginning of WWII, which
had a great impact on reduced number of delegates (see Table 1.2).
The CIGRE organisation has reinforced its position in the period up to 1939 as
the leading technical organisation for the field of electrical supply industry
(ESI) in the world.
The first three National Committees were established in 1923 (UK, NL, IT) and
nine more NC’s after establishing the independent organization: Belgium,
France, Denmark, Japan, USA, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland. In
1932, Germany NC CIGRE was established, which attended the Session for the
first time in 1933. In 1935, German NC was included, but in 1939 excluded again,
and in 1952 approved again. Today, German NC CIGRE is one of the most active
committee with the largest number of honorary members.

After the Second World War, CIGRE organised the 11th Conference in Paris
already as early as June of 1946. It was the first technical organisation in the
world that activated its membership after the Second World War. Europe was
in ruins, so all levels of the profession had to be activated quickly to set up a
new era of electrification. Despite huge problems with transport across Europe,
877 delegates from 30 countries attended the first post-war CIGRE Conference.


18
             Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




Next decade was marked with constantly increasing interest for participation
at CIGRE Sessions.

12th Session in Paris in 1948 attended 1144 delegates from 40 countries – over
1000 delegates for the first time at CIGRE Sessions. That was the time, when
for the first time in history, a 400 kV cable was presented and was later put
into operation in Sweden (in 1952). Figure 1.4 presents the development of the
OHL’s voltages growth, much like interconnection networks. Nominal voltage
400 kV (380 kV) was designed as early as in the 1930’s, as the basic voltage of
the pan-European network, but realized later in 1950’s.




         Fig. 1.4 Development of voltage levels from 15 kV to 1150 kV (1891–1985)

At the time, a number of new Study Committees were organised, namely SC7
– for poles, foundations and engineering of overhead power lines, SC9 – for AC
Transmissions of very high voltages, SC10 – for DC Transmissions of very high
voltages, SC11 – for telephone and radio interferences, and SC12 – for stability
and regulation of frequency. From the names of the new Study Committees it
is evident, that the electric power system began to expand quickly and that new
problems began to accumulate, which required solutions. Due to the vast inter-
est of experts, who wished to participate in the international Study Committees,


                                                                                           19
SEERC CIGRE HISTORY




this was the first time that the number of regular members of Study Commit-
tees had to be limited to 12 members. Today’s limit is 30 regular members.

The period 1946–1950 could be marked as the third milestone (see sub-chapter
1.3) in history of CIGRE.
Interestingly, CIGRE membership fee at that time depended on the production
of electricity by a country member. Payment method was later changed.
Thus, over a decade after WWII, the number of participating countries jumped
to 50 and the number of delegates exceeded 1500. (Table 1.3).

CIGRE also started publishing CIGRE journal called Electra. First version of
Electra was issued in 1931 (15th June), several days before legendary 6th Session.
This version was also used for SC minutes and other administrative informa-
tion. During second milestone of CIGRE in 1967, when second reform of or-
ganization started, ELECTRA magazine also changed the design. President
of CIGRE at that time was Andrew R. Cooper from UK, and Vice-President
and Delegate General, Professor Francois Cahen. In 1967, the first issue of new
Electra was published. During that period, magazine changed a lot, but always
tried to stay closer to members.

Jean Tribot Laspiere was the Secretary General or so called Delegate General
at that time, and “spiritus agens” of the organisation, ever since its foundation
and up to the year 1963. Posthumously, he was proclaimed as the Founder of
the CIGRE. Over 40 years, Jean Tribot Laspiere organised all CIGRE events
from 1921 up to 1963.
Later, Professor Francois Cahen took on the role of Delegate General or Secre-
tary General and the main CIGRE organizer, who at this critical time carried
out extremely successful reforms for the organization. At the same time, this
was the period of fastest growth in electricity systems in Europe, which in

1.3 History of CIGRE Leaders

In a century old history of CIGRE, the most important for sure were the gov-
ernors: President and Secretary General. Table 1.7 presents the chronology of
CIGRE Presidents since 1921 and table 1.8 presents chronology of Secretaries
General as head of professional staff in Central office in Paris.

CIGRE’s history could be defined by some critical periods as milestones, when
crucial organizational changes and improvements were made. This book de-
fines 6 such periods, as follows:
  A. 1921, creation of conference and first conference, which gave the
     acronym CIGRE,
  B. 1931, when CIGRE was established as independent International
     organization,
  C. 1946–1963, after WW2, when period of intensive electrification and
     interconnection of power systems worldwide started,
  D. 1963–1974, period after death of CIGRE’s founder, Jean Tribot Laspiere
  E. 1998–2002, re-organization of CIGRE and new SCs’ structure for 21st
     century
  F. 2014–2018, opening CIGRE to the whole electric power sector as a
     reaction to global changes of the energy sector in the direction of
     decarbonization and clean energy for all.

2. CIGRE GLOBAL REGIONS
Organization of the regions is a novelty of the global institution CIGRE, which
started in the year 2000. However, before that, there have been a lot of discus-
sions about this topic in the CIGRE Administrative council. In 1998, Ad Hoc
group was set up for making analyses on modernization of the institutional
arrangements, considering possibilities of regions, advantages, and disadvan-
tages of that solution. Ad Hoc group recommended to National Committees,
to form the regional CIGRE entities, among geographically related members.
Soon afterwards, following regional CIGRE councils have been established:
  • In 2000, AORC – CIGRE (Asia-Oceania Regional Council of CIGRE),
  • In 2001, NRCC – CIGRE (Nordic Regional Council of CIGRE),
  • In 2006, RIAC – CIGRE (Regional Ibero-American of CIGRE), and
  • In 2013, SEERC – CIGRE (South-East European Region of CIGRE).
Later, regions are included in the new version of CIGRE Statue – Article 17 with
following wording:
REGIONS
National Committees may come together to form a Region, which is a set-up designed to
enhance technical cooperation between countries and to promote and develop CIGRE.
Geographical proximity is the primary motive for forming a Region, but other situations
can be accommodated when they fall in with the basic objectives, i.e.:
  a. Contribute to the activities of the Study Committees, addressing and developing
      local issues;
  b. Organize Regional Meetings or other local meetings (Colloquia…);
  c. Coordinate with industry organizations.
  d. Coordinate contributions to CIGRE main events (Session, Symposia);
  e. Encourage and provide an incentive to increase CIGRE membership and create
      new National
Committees, by incorporating countries without a National Committee in the working
structure.
The existence of Regions has no impact on the governance structure of CIGRE - National
Committees, Administrative Council, and Steering Committee - nor does it introduce
any hierarchical notion in relations with National Committees or Study Committees.

2.1 AORC – Asia and Oceania Regional Council of CIGRE

Members of AORC are CIGRE NC’s of Australia, China, India, Indonesia, Japan,
South Korea, Malaysia, New Zealand, and Thailand. In 2014, AORC published
the book “AORC-CIGRE History” Electricity empowering the Region, where
three new CIGRE NC’s were announced to join this region and they are as fol-
lows Iran, Jordan and Gulf Cooperation Countries (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Unit-
ed Arab Emirates, Qatar, Bahrain and Oman). Taiwan, Macau, and Hong Kong
participate as observers. This exceptionally large CIGRE region is composed of
12 CIGRE National Committees and three observing members.


28
              Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




AORC – CIGRE was the first established region of CIGRE. Administrative Coun-
cil members from Australia, China, India, Japan, and Malaysia agreed to form
a “Region” called AORC-CIGRE, and that Japanese NC took over the role of
preparing the initial blueprints of the constitution and working procedures.
In May 2000, Constitutional meeting in Kuala Lumpur was held, where they
determined draft of the statute, the action plan and selected JNC CIGRE to first
take the lead (Mr. Tadao Amakasu as first Chairman and Mr. Hiroshi Suzuki
as Secretary). The management mandate (chairman and secretary) lasts two
years. Every year AORC organizes council meetings with representatives of
all members’ states, panels on different technical issues (i.e. panel B1, B2) and
Task forces.


2.2 RIAC – Regional Ibero-American of CIGRE

Members of RIAC are CIGRE NC’s of Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay, Andes (Bo-
livia, Equator, and Peru), Columbia, Chile, Spain, Mexico, and Portugal. All
together 9 National Committees in 12 countries.
In Latin America CIGRE meetings of active experts in CIGRE started in 1986.
Those meetings were called ERLAC (El Encuentro Regional Iberoamericano de
CIGRE). In 2003, during regional meeting of ERLAC (Regional Meeting of Latin
American CIGRE members) in Argentina, members (at that time Argentina,
Brazil, Spain, Portugal, Mexico, Venezuela, and Paraguay) agreed to establish
CIGRE Region and apply for official registration in CIGRE Paris. In August
2004, Administrative Council of CIGRE approved new region of RIAC (Regione
Ibero America de CIGRE). Due to establishment of the third CIGRE region, Ad-
ministrative Council of CIGRE submitted some changing of the Statute, which
was approved on general Assembly in August 2006.
In May 2005, there was an inaugural meeting of RIAC in Paraguay. Basic ar-
guments for initiative of RIAC were:
  • work carried out jointly to promote CIGRE activities in Latin America,
  • cultural identity,
  • affinity for the two sister languages of the region (Portuguese and Spanish),
  • knowledge of experts from these countries, and
  • the possibility of developing a promising geographical area for CIGRE.
The objectives of the RIAC were:
  • strengthening the ties of the Technological Union and disseminating in-
      formation on electricity related issues between Latin American states,


                                                                                            29
SEERC CIGRE HISTORY




  • integrate all Latin American states into CIGRE network.
Result of these activities were the establishment of the Chilean NC CIGRE in
2003 and the Andean Committee in 2006 (Bolivia, Colombia, Ecuador, and
Peru).
The leadership of RIAC (as available information from 2013) were:
  • Chairman: Jorge Alberto Nizovoy (Argentina)
  • Vice-chairman: Luis Imaz (Spain)
  • Secretary: Oscar Ribeiro (Portugal)
  • Vice-secretary: Helio Pereira (Paraguay)
  • Chairman of Technical body: Ruy Menezes (Brazil).
RIAC organize Technical meetings in the scale of Paris Sessions. In addition,
there are plenary Sessions and poster and exhibition on equipment and systems
related to the electricity sector. The growth of the participants is continuous.
The official languages are English, Portuguese, and Spanish.


2.3 NRCC – Nordic Regional Council of CIGRE

Members of NRCC are the CIGRE NC’s of Denmark, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania,
Finland, Island, Norway, and Sweden.
Representatives of NRCC members organize at least one meeting every year,
discussing CIGRE issues. Council leadership transfers on the duties after every
annual meeting.
NRCC does not organize regional technical events like conference or symposia.
Organization of workshops, colloquium or symposia is a subject of the National
Committee organization.

The main tasks of the Nordic regional council of CIGRE are:
 • Work to achieve added value to the individual National Committees in
    the Region,
 • Building up CIGRE activities in an enlarged geographical area, and in-
    crease the interaction between experts from countries in the Region, and
 • Stimulate activities at the regional level (Symposia, Colloquia, etc.) with
    a lower financial risk exposure and greater attendance, compared to an
    activity based solely on one nation.

              Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




2.4 SEERC – South-East European Region of CIGRE

Members of SEERC are the National CIGRE committees of Austria, Bosnia/
Herzegovina, Croatia, Czech/Slovak Republics, Georgia, Greece, Italy, Israel,
Kosovo, North Macedonia, Montenegro, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, Turkey,
and Ukraine. All together 17 countries, 16 NC CIGRE (Czech and Slovak Republic
operate as one NC). Hungary is still a pending member, although it was active
from the beginning of establishing SEERC region and belongs to this region.

3. HISTORY OF SEERC 2005–2020
3.1 The early years

First discussion about closer regional cooperation of National CIGRE Commit-
tees in the South-East Europe began during Administrative Council of CIGRE
in 2005, in Bangalore (India). Amongst the representatives from Greece, Italy,
Slovenia and others from central and southern Europe, an idea had developed
to establish a new regional council, in accordance with CIGRE rules for better
understanding of each other, better cooperation inside CIGRE family, particu-
larly after hearing about the good results from already operating AORC CIGRE
Region. After first informal discussion, quite a few years passed, until the first
meeting happened. The president of the Slovenian NC CIGRE Kresimir Bakic
invited the representatives of National Committees from Italy, Austria, Hun-
gary, Croatia, Bosnia, Montenegro, Macedonia, Serbia, Greece, and Romania
to Kranjska Gora, Alpine area of Slovenia, to meet and continue the discussion
on possibilities of establishing CIGRE region in that part of Europe, on May 26,
2009. In the light of future development of electric power systems and CIGRE
broad activities, he proposed a friendly discussion on common regional chal-
lenges in power sector and better cooperation between National Committees.
Representatives from seven countries: Austria, Italy, Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia
and Herzegovina, Hungary and Slovenia attended the meeting. Representatives
from Greece, Romania, Montenegro, and Macedonia apologized and expressed
interest to join this idea. The focus of the meeting was exchanging experiences
and analysing mutual interests for better cooperation in accordance with CIGRE
rules and spirit of CIGRE. Each NC presented its own position of interest. Dur-
ing the meeting, draft of Statute was also presented, like already existing ones
in other CIGRE regions.

The result of the meeting was positive, but still with some doubts about organ-
izing models and program framework as well as some political issues, which
they tried to avoid following the CIGRE spirit. During the CIGRE Adminis-
trative Council in Seoul (Korea), a few representatives asked Kresimir Bakic
(Slovenia) to organize second informal meeting during the CIGRE Session in
Paris, in 2012.
Thus, in 2012 after Administrative Council meeting in Paris representatives of
NCs continued the discussion about new CIGRE Region with one more country.
Mr. Yuriy Bondarenko from NC CIGRE of Ukraine expressed interest to join
this region and participate in all activities.
President of NC CIGRE Montenegro, professor Milutin Ostojic, invited repre-
sentatives of all countries of interest to Montenegro next year to finalize all
strives on founding new CIGRE Region. President of CIGRE, Professor Klaus
Fröhlich strongly supported these activities of National Committees to find
suitable model for intensive collaboration inside the mother organization of
CIGRE. In 2012, there came to a final decision in a meeting in Paris, to invite
all interested National Committees of CIGRE from Central, South, and Eastern
Europe to the founding conference in May 2013, in Montenegro.


3.2 Founding conference of SEERC CIGRE Region

Communication between the members in 2012 continued through e-mails,
trying to solve some non-technical issues. In March 2013, president of CIGRE,
Klaus Fröhlich, wrote a letter to Kresimir Bakic, NCs group organizer, stress-
ing attention to following aspects for creation and recognition of new CIGRE
Region:
  a. CIGRE Region needs to be officially recognized by Administrative
     Council (AM).
  b. Statute of the Region should be strictly in coordination with CIGRE
     regulations.
Thus, the steps for beginning of the process were defined by:
  • Mutual agreement as Memorandum of Understanding (MoU),
  • Application for recognition to Administrative Council of CIGRE and set
     up working program.

3.3 SEERC Memorandum of Understanding

SEERC Memorandum of Understanding, was approved by members, as the
base document for establishing new CIGRE Region, contains the following:

 1. Formation
Based on a common interest and former informal co-operation, the National Com-
mittees of CIGRE in Austria, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Croatia, Greece, Hungary, Italy,
Macedonia, Montenegro, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia and Ukraine decided to set up a
new Regional CIGRE council operating under the name SOUTH EAST EUROPEAN
REGION of CIGRE (SEERC). The regional council was formed according to the statutes
of CIGRE and will be endorsed as a region of CIGRE by the Administrative Council of
CIGRE at the meeting in September 2013 in Kazan (Russia).

 2. Objectives
The objectives of the SEERC are:
  • Work to achieve added value to the individual NC in the Region,
  • Build up CIGRE activities in an enlarged geographical area and increase the in-
     teraction between experts from countries in the Region,
  • Promote activities (Symposia, Colloquia, etc.) with a lower financial risk exposure
     and greater attendance, compared to an activity based solely on one national
     Committee,
  • Promote and nurture new National committees in the Region,
  • Encourage new regional activities in correlation with new energy policy and large
     regional energy projects.

 3. Methods
The SEERC achieves its objectives by appropriate methods and actions, which are in
accordance with the policies of CIGRE.
The methods and actions of the SEERC include, but are not limited to, the following:
  • A yearly regional meeting is held between the chairman of the National Commit-
      tees and the members of the Administrative Council from these countries. Topics
      for such meetings are:
     • Information about activities within each country,
     • Co-operation in the Study Committee level,
     • Co-ordination of proposals for new SC members,
     • Discussion of nomination of CIGRE officers,



                                                                                             37
SEERC CIGRE HISTORY




    • Discussion of specific Regional issues,
    • Discussion on action plan,
    • Update of the statutes and rules governing the activities of SEERC when needs
        arises. Such updating requires that the members of SEERC unanimously agree
        on these changes.
  • The location of the meeting rotates among the member countries. Also, it is possible
     to organize meetings before or after CIGRE Administrative Committee annual
     meetings

 4. Member of the Region
The founding members of SEERC are NC’s of Bosnia & Herzegovina, Croatia, Italy,
Macedonia, Montenegro, Romania, Serbia, Slovenia, and Ukraine. These partici-
pants will promote CIGRE membership to the countries which doesn’t have national
committee at the present time. A new country in the region can be approved as full
member of SEERC at the annual meeting of this organization if the country in question
has a National Committee fulfilling the requirements of CIGRE.
Each member carries one vote in the case of making decisions by voting.

 5. Application
Application for participation should be sent to the chairman of SEERC as an attachment
or with a reference to document the applicant’s status as “Having a national Committee
fulfilling the requirements of CIGRE”. According to SEERC’s statutes this is a require-
ment for joining the region.

 6. Chairmanship
The mandate period for the chairman of the SEERC is two years.
The chairmanship rotates among member countries in alphabetical order of NC or as
agreed at the annual meetings. Starting chairmanship in 2013 will be Kresimir Bakic.

 7. Secretary of SEERC
To assist the SEERC in practical matters like
  • Organising meetings of SEERC, issuing agenda and material prior to meetings,
      preparing minutes from meetings,
  • Communicating with CIGRE’s Central Office in administrative matters,
SEERC has a secretary who will be appointed by the country which is to take over the
chairmanship. This procedure is based on the idea that holding the secretariat in a
period immediately before taking over the chairmanship will help to ensure continuity.
  • Web Site of SEERC


38
               Early electrification and empowerment of region where current electricity was born




 8. Meetings
Apart from the yearly meeting, meetings can be called upon request of any member of
the SEERC. Such a request should be sent to the chairman with motivation and sug-
gested agenda. Meetings must be announced no later than one month before being held.
Material for the meeting must be sent to participants no later than one week before the
meeting. Decision on issues not on the agenda can only be made if all members are
present and all accept that a decision can be made. Decisions are preferably reached by
consensus. Failing that, decision can be made by simple majority. Changes of statutes
require unanimity as specified in the statutes. Minutes from the meetings should nor-
mally reach participants no later than three weeks after a meeting. Minutes should be
brief and mainly include decisions. It is left to participants to record details.

 9. Information Exchange
To facilitate information exchange between members and to facilitate information pro-
vision for interested external parties, SEERC maintains its website. The website should
allow members and candidate’s members to keep up-to-date information about:
SEERC, Statutes, Membership, Key persons, for each member and aggregated, mem-
bership status, Study Committee chairman, Study Committee members, WG and TF
members, activities of potential interest to SEERC members, proposed papers to the
Paris CIGRE Sessions and other CIGRE events

 10. Finances and Organization
The financial principle is that each National Committee should bear its own costs. Thus,
no money will be allocated to the SEERC as such. The work within the region should
be carried out without establishing any bureaucracy. The National Committees should
continue their activities and maintain their status. All correspondence from CIGRE
should go directly to the National Committees. The SEERC will keep the CIGRE Central
Office informed of its activities and of changes in chairmanship as they occur.
Approved and signed by representatives of NC CIGRE by countries (9):
R. Mahmutćehaić (Bosnia and Herzegovina), B. Filipović-Grčić (Croatia), M.
Rebolini (Italy), R. Taleski (Macedonia), M. Ostojić (Montenegro), I. Hategan
(Romania), D. Dotlić (Serbia), K. Bakič (Slovenia) and Y. Bondarenko (Ukraine).
